threats.name: Temporal discontinuity, rather than forgery evidence, drives video detection

threats.name: Accuracy differences are driven by class composition or the chosen threshold

threats.name: Manipulation-specific changes in augmentation create an unintended cue

threats.name: A localization metric rewards mask size rather than explanation quality

controls.name: No-augmentation condition
controls.detail: The paper compares training with all augmentations against training without any augmentations.
controls.rules_out: Whether observed performance changes require the augmentation pipeline rather than occurring without augmentation.

controls.detail: The paper compares training with all augmentations against conditions omitting a specific augmentation, including rotations, horizontal flips, image compression, isotropic scaling, color jitter, and Gaussian blur.

controls.name: ResNet without depthwise separable convolution
controls.detail: The paper compares ResNet with ResNet-DSC, which adds a depthwise separable convolution module by replacing the first convolutional layer.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported ResNet-DSC improvement occurs without adding that module.

controls.name: Non-pre-trained backbone

controls.rules_out: Whether the measured performance difference depends on pre-trained weights.

confounds.name: Apparent detector-method advantage is due to training factors rather than the method itself
confounds.detail: The paper notes that performance gaps between advanced methods and naive detectors could result from factors such as pre-training, data augmentation, or the number of training frames, rather than intrinsic method superiority.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It analyzes augmentation effects using Xception and SPSL, compares pre-trained with non-pre-trained Xception, EfficientNet-B4, and ResNet34, and identifies the number of training frames as a factor for analysis.

confounds.name: Backbone performance differences are explained by model scale or particular architectural components
confounds.detail: The paper considers whether the advantage of Xception and EfficientNet-B4 over ResNet34 reflects depthwise separable convolution or differences in model scale, rather than backbone choice alone.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It notes comparable parameter counts, inserts depthwise separable convolution into ResNet and evaluates ResNet-DSC, and examines ResNet variants with different layer counts.

datasets.name: ForgeryNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Image- and video-level sets are split into train/validation/test at approximately 7:1:2, with identities matched between real and fake subsets and real:fake approximately 1:1. For intra-forgery classification, train on the training set and evaluate on validation data, using two-, three-, or n-way labels (n=16 for images, n=9 for videos). For cross-forgery classification, train on one manipulation type and test on other types; the type may be a meta-category or a specific approach. Spatial localization trains on images and forgery masks; the paper does not specify the evaluation split. Temporal localization results are reported on the validation set. Image experiments use face crops from bounding boxes enlarged by 1.3× and training augmentations intended to mimic compression and packet loss. Video classification samples 16 frames at temporal stride 4; binary results are reported with single-crop and multi-crop strategies. Classification uses accuracy and AUC for binary tasks and accuracy and mAP for three-/n-way tasks; temporal localization uses interpolated AP and AR@K.

controls.name: Separate-task training
controls.detail: Train separate models for FAS and face-forgery detection rather than one jointly trained model.
controls.rules_out: That the reported joint-training differences are simply the performance of the tasks without joint training.

controls.name: MSTmap-only rPPG input
controls.detail: Use the time-domain MSTmap without the WaveletMap branch, compared with the two-branch MSTmap-plus-WaveletMap model.
controls.rules_out: That the two-branch model's gains occur without the added time-frequency representation.

controls.name: Direct concatenation, SE fusion, and cross-attention fusion
controls.detail: Compare these feature-fusion strategies with the proposed weighted batch/layer normalization fusion.
controls.rules_out: That the weighted-normalization result is merely the result of combining appearance and rPPG features or using a fusion operator, rather than the particular normalization strategy.

controls.name: Only extra bonafides or only extra attacks
controls.detail: Compare joint training with both tasks' bonafides and attacks against conditions that add only bonafides or only attacks from the other task.
controls.rules_out: That the observed joint-training performance requires, or is explained solely by, adding just one of those sample types.

controls.name: Joint training with unrelated face-analysis tasks on RAF-DB
controls.detail: Compare FAS-plus-forgery joint training with joint training that adds expression, gender, or race recognition.
controls.rules_out: That gains arise merely from adding more face data or another task, rather than from the relationship between FAS and forgery detection.

controls.name: Alternative task-sampling schedules
controls.detail: Compare random minibatch sampling with simultaneous, alternating, and task-by-task sampling.
controls.rules_out: That the result attributed to random task sampling is independent of how batches from the two tasks are scheduled.

controls.name: Alternative joint heads and sharing configurations
controls.detail: Evaluate different classification-head settings and different numbers of shared backbone blocks alongside the stated joint-training configurations.
controls.rules_out: That joint-training results are independent of the head design or the extent of backbone sharing.

confounds.name: Joint-training gains come from extra data volume rather than task correlation
confounds.detail: The headline gains could occur simply because joint training supplies more face data, even if FAS and face-forgery detection are not especially related.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Jointly train with expression, gender, or race recognition using RAF-DB as an additional face-analysis task and measure attack-detection and auxiliary-task accuracy; the paper reports limited gains for these tasks and performance drops in some settings, unlike the FAS-plus-forgery results.

metrics.caveat: High accuracy on a test set with a distribution close to training may not indicate real-world performance; the paper also evaluates accuracy on a hidden test set with unknown manipulation methods and diverse distortions.

metrics.name: Five-level video realness rating and percentage rated “real”

controls.name: Standard set without distortions (std)
controls.detail: The paper compares training/evaluation conditions that add single-level, random-level, or mixed distortions against the undistorted standard set.
controls.rules_out: A measured improvement over std supports an effect from adding the distortion-augmented training data rather than merely using the standard training condition.

confounds.name: Close training–test distribution inflates apparent real-world detection performance
confounds.detail: The authors note that standard test sets sharing a close distribution with training can yield high accuracy even when models may fail on real-world fakes.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on the hidden test set, whose fakes use unknown swapping methods, diverse hidden distortions, and are selected for fooling human observers.

confounds.name: Temporal discontinuity in generated fakes may explain high video-level detection accuracy
confounds.detail: The authors conjecture that temporal discontinuity in fake videos leads to higher accuracy for I3D on the standard training set.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No specific measurement ruling this explanation out is reported.

evidence_standards.name: Human ratings from 100 professional participants
evidence_standards.detail: For the user study, 30 randomly selected clips per dataset are rated on a five-level scale; ratings of 4 or 5 are counted as “real.” Hidden-test fakes are selected if at least 50 of 100 observers are fooled. The paper does not state a statistical test, repeated runs, or a variance-based rule for deciding model-accuracy differences.

datasets.name: FaceForensics++ (FF++)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the official subject-independent 720:140:140 train/validation/test split; testing follows the official test split. Uses the HQ (c23) version when applicable. The reported test set has 140 real and 560 fake videos. Common preprocessing extracts and crops faces; frame-level detectors use N=20 test frames per video, and their face-level results are averaged to a video-level output.

datasets.name: Deepfake Detection Challenge (DFDC)
datasets.eval_protocol: Randomly selects 10 of the 50 official video folders, then randomly shuffles and selects 100 real and 100 fake videos from each folder. Manually examines the selected fake videos and removes pure-audio-swap fakes. Evaluates on 1,000 real and 1,000 fake videos after the common face preprocessing; frame-level detectors use N=20 test frames per video and face-level results are averaged to video-level outputs.

datasets.name: Celeb-DF
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates on the official testing set of 178 real and 340 fake videos. Applies the common face preprocessing; frame-level detectors use N=20 test frames per video and face-level results are averaged to video-level outputs.

datasets.name: DeeperForensics-1.0 (DF1.0)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the official 7:1:2 split for fake videos and evaluates only the fake test videos (described as 2,000 in the text; Table 3 reports 2,010). Applies the common face preprocessing; frame-level detectors use N=20 test frames per video and face-level results are averaged to video-level outputs.

datasets.name: FaceShifter
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates only the 140 fake videos corresponding to the FF++ official test split; the shared real videos are not included. Applies the common face preprocessing; frame-level detectors use N=20 test frames per video and face-level results are averaged to video-level outputs.

baselines.name: Xception
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmark test sets with common preprocessing and video-level ACC/AUC. The authors use published optimal parameter settings; models without directly adopted trained weights are trained on FF++ under the paper's stated setup.

baselines.name: MAT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmark test sets with common preprocessing and video-level ACC/AUC. The authors use published optimal parameter settings; models without directly adopted trained weights are trained on FF++ under the paper's stated setup.

baselines.name: RECCE
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmark test sets with common preprocessing and video-level ACC/AUC. The authors use published optimal parameter settings; models without directly adopted trained weights are trained on FF++ under the paper's stated setup.

baselines.name: Stage5
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmark test sets with common preprocessing and video-level ACC/AUC. The authors use published optimal parameter settings and directly adopt available trained weights where the paper's stated conditions apply.

baselines.name: FSTMatching
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmark test sets with common preprocessing and video-level ACC/AUC. The authors use published optimal parameter settings; models without directly adopted trained weights are trained on FF++ under the paper's stated setup.

baselines.name: MetricLearning
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmark test sets with common preprocessing and video-level ACC/AUC. The authors use published optimal parameter settings and directly adopt available trained weights where the paper's stated conditions apply.

baselines.name: LRNet
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmark test sets with common preprocessing and video-level ACC/AUC. The authors use published optimal parameter settings and directly adopt available trained weights where the paper's stated conditions apply.

metrics.name: Accuracy (ACC)
metrics.caveat: The classification threshold is fixed at 0.5 for the reported accuracy, although the optimal threshold may differ across models and test sets; the paper reports AUC alongside ACC to show separability beyond that fixed threshold.

metrics.name: AUC score
metrics.caveat: AUC does not indicate performance at the fixed 0.5 classification threshold, and the paper notes that a useful classification threshold may vary across test sets and models. It is inapplicable when a test set contains only one class; the paper also reports ACC.

confounds.name: The fixed classification threshold, rather than weak real/fake discrimination, may explain low accuracy
confounds.detail: The paper notes that accuracy uses a threshold of 0.5 even though the optimal threshold may be elsewhere, so a model can have low ACC despite distinguishing real from fake.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report AUC alongside ACC; the paper uses MetricLearning's higher AUC despite its 50% accuracy as an example of this distinction.

confounds.name: Class composition of the reliability sample may affect accuracy
confounds.detail: The sampling frame contains more fake than real videos, so unrestricted random samples can contain more fake items and shift accuracy depending on performance on fake samples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Run and report both balanced sampling and fully random imbalanced sampling, comparing their accuracy intervals; this measures sensitivity to sampling composition rather than eliminating it.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated random-sampling confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: For the reliability study, use 500 and 3,000 sampling trials at sample sizes 10, 100, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, and 2,500, with both balanced and imbalanced sampling. Report the trial mean, standard deviation, and 90% and 95% confidence intervals, calculated using a normal-distribution z-score and the central limit theorem. No statistical significance test, seed count, or no-difference margin is specified.

evidence_standards.name: Real-life case-study frame sampling
evidence_standards.detail: For frame-level detectors, randomly extract 100 faces per video when enough face-containing frames are available; the cheerleader news clip has 75 available faces. Report the detector outputs and the corresponding balanced-sampling 95% accuracy confidence intervals.

datasets.name: GenImage
datasets.eval_protocol: The benchmark has 1,000 ImageNet classes; real images are split into 1,281,167 training and 50,000 test images. Each of eight generator subsets has training and test images across the 1,000 classes (generally 162 training and 6 test images per class per generator; SD V1.5 uses 166 and 8). The paper reports binary classification accuracy. For cross-generator evaluation, it trains on SD V1.4 and tests on each of the eight generator subsets, averaging the eight accuracies; it also reports results from eight models trained on the eight generators, averaged over 64 train/test combinations. For degraded-image evaluation, it trains on SD V1.4 and degrades only test images: downsampling to 112 or 64, JPEG quality 65 or 30, and Gaussian blur with σ=3 or 5.

datasets.name: LFW
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 10,000 real face images and 10,000 fake face images generated with SD V1.4 using face labels from LFW. A detector trained on the GenImage SD V1.4 subset is evaluated on the test data without fine-tuning; reports accuracy.

datasets.name: Laion-Art
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 10,000 real art images and 10,000 fake art images generated with SD V1.4 using prompts from DiffusionDB. A detector trained on the GenImage SD V1.4 subset is evaluated on the test data without fine-tuning; reports accuracy.

baselines.name: ResNet-50
baselines.fair_comparison: For the SD V1.4 cross-generator comparison, trained on SD V1.4 and evaluated on the same eight generator test subsets as the other methods. In the eight-model cross-validation comparison, trained one model per generator and averaged the 64 train/test results.

baselines.name: DeiT-S
baselines.fair_comparison: For the SD V1.4 cross-generator comparison, trained on SD V1.4 and evaluated on the same eight generator test subsets as the other methods. In the eight-model cross-validation comparison, trained one model per generator and averaged the 64 train/test results.

baselines.name: Swin-T
baselines.fair_comparison: For the SD V1.4 cross-generator comparison, trained on SD V1.4 and evaluated on the same eight generator test subsets as the other methods. In the eight-model cross-validation comparison, trained one model per generator and averaged the 64 train/test results.

baselines.name: CNNSpot
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside the other methods after training on the paper's dataset; for the SD V1.4 cross-generator comparison, trained on SD V1.4 and tested on the same eight generator subsets. Its training uses blur and JPEG augmentation.

baselines.name: Spec
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside the other methods after training on the paper's dataset; for the SD V1.4 cross-generator comparison, trained on SD V1.4 and tested on the same eight generator subsets.

baselines.name: F3Net
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside the other methods after training on the paper's dataset; for the SD V1.4 cross-generator comparison, trained on SD V1.4 and tested on the same eight generator subsets.

baselines.name: GramNet
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated alongside the other methods after training on the paper's dataset; for the SD V1.4 cross-generator comparison, trained on SD V1.4 and tested on the same eight generator subsets.

confounds.name: High accuracy may depend on generator-specific cues rather than general fake-image cues
confounds.detail: The paper notes that a detector trained on one generator may be tied to that generator and perform poorly on unknown generators.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It evaluates a detector trained on SD V1.4 on all eight generator test subsets, and also reports cross-validation across eight train/test generators. The reported transfer drops show that generator-specific dependence is not ruled out.

confounds.name: Performance may depend on image classes or content rather than generalizing across image content
confounds.detail: The paper explicitly evaluates whether detectors trained on a subset of image classes generalize to other classes and whether a GenImage-trained detector works on face and art images.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It trains on subsets of 10, 50, or 100 classes and tests across 1,000 classes; it also tests on LFW face images and Laion-Art images without fine-tuning.

datasets.name: AI-GenBench
datasets.eval_protocol: 36 generators are ordered by release date into 9 sliding windows of 4 generators. Each generator has 4K training images and 1K evaluation images; real images are split 80/20 and partitioned into groups associated with generators. At step k, train incrementally on all windows through k (1 epoch per step, with training augmentation multiplier 4). Evaluate with deterministic augmentation on Past Period (windows through k), Next Period (window k+1), and Whole Period (windows through k+1). Report AUROC and accuracy; leaderboard ranking uses their averages across steps for Next Period. Evaluation augmentation includes compression, blurring, noise, variable resizing, and cropping.

baselines.name: ResNet-50 CLIP (OpenAI)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated under the shared AI-GenBench workflow: 224×224 inputs, one epoch per incremental step, and the same training/evaluation data and augmentation constraints. The paper tests fine-tuning and linear probing, with resize and multi-crop input adaptation.

baselines.name: ViT-L/14 CLIP (LAION, CLIP-ViT-L-14-CommonPool.XL-s13B-b90K)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated under the shared AI-GenBench workflow: 224×224 inputs, one epoch per incremental step, and the same training/evaluation data and augmentation constraints. The paper tests fine-tuning and linear probing, with resize and multi-crop input adaptation.

baselines.name: ViT-L/14 DINOv2
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated under the shared AI-GenBench workflow: 224×224 inputs, one epoch per incremental step, and the same training/evaluation data and augmentation constraints. The paper tests fine-tuning and linear probing, with resize and multi-crop input adaptation.

confounds.name: Performance gains could come from using more augmentation and computational resources rather than a better detection method
confounds.detail: The paper notes that methods using more extensive augmentation could perform better simply by spending more resources.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The training augmentation multiplier is fixed at 4 augmented versions per training image, and evaluation augmentation is deterministic and fixed.

confounds.name: Apparent generalization could result from arbitrary rather than genuinely future-facing train/test splits
confounds.detail: The paper identifies arbitrary splits as a source of biased or unreliable outcomes; testing on generators already represented in training would not establish generalization to newly released generators.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Generators are ordered by release date and evaluated in chronological windows: at step k, training uses windows through k and Next Period evaluation uses the unseen window k+1.

datasets.name: Deepfake dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: The authors’ internet-video dataset: 175 forged rushes, with real face images collected from internet sources. They report a held-out test set of 2,889 forged and 4,259 real face images; 10% of the training set was used for validation. Frame-level classification is reported, with video-level scores also reported by averaging predictions over a video. Faces were extracted with Viola–Jones and aligned using a neural-network facial-landmark detector; inputs were 256×256×3. Videos were H.264-compressed, and the authors matched the classes’ distributions of good- and poor-resolution images as much as possible.

datasets.name: FaceForensics dataset (Face2Face)
datasets.eval_protocol: Used the dataset’s existing train/validation/test split; 300 videos were used for training, and evaluation used 150 forged test videos and their originals (3,000 extracted face images per class). 10% of training data was used for validation. Frame-level classification was evaluated at H.264 compression levels 0 (lossless), 23 (light), and 40 (strong); video-level aggregation was also reported at level 23. Inputs were 256×256×3.

baselines.name: Xception
baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tuned using the configuration from the FaceForensics paper; the authors report results on FaceForensics at compression levels 0 and 23. Further details of matched training or evaluation conditions are not stated.

metrics.name: classification score
metrics.caveat: Frame predictions from the same video are strongly correlated, so the authors say video aggregation has no theoretical justification as a gain or confidence-interval indicator; they also report video-level scores using averaged frame predictions.

metrics.name: aggregation score
metrics.caveat: Frames from the same video are strongly correlated, so the authors caution that an aggregation gain does not have a theoretically justified confidence-interval interpretation.

confounds.name: Resolution differences between forged and real images could bias Deepfake classification
confounds.detail: A classifier might use image-resolution quality rather than forgery cues, producing an apparent detection result.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors say they matched the distributions of good- and poor-resolution images across the forged and real classes as much as possible.

confounds.name: Compression level could account for Face2Face classification performance
confounds.detail: Detection might depend on compression artifacts rather than forgery cues, making performance specific to a compression setting.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors evaluated FaceForensics at lossless, light (23), and strong (40) H.264 compression and reported the resulting scores.

datasets.name: CDDB
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate three sequential task streams, training on each task in order and evaluating on the associated test data: EASY = GauGAN, BigGAN, CycleGAN, IMLE, FaceForensic++, CRN, WildDeepfake; HARD = GauGAN, BigGAN, WildDeepfake, WhichFaceReal, SAN; LONG = GauGAN, BigGAN, CycleGAN, IMLE, FaceForensic++, CRN, WildDeepfake, Glow, StarGAN, StyleGAN, WhichFaceReal, SAN. ProGAN and corresponding real samples may be used for warm-up pretraining. WildDeepfake videos are represented by randomly selected frames. The paper does not specify train/validation/test split details in the supplied text. It reports AA, AF, mAP, and, for multiclass methods, AA-M; exemplar-based methods use a 1500-example memory in the main evaluations, with reduced-memory evaluations on HARD.

datasets.name: GANfake
datasets.eval_protocol: Also studied in the supplementary material using the authors’ own splits, following the original paper’s description; the original detailed train/validation/test splits are not released. Further protocol details are not given in the supplied text.

baselines.name: CNNDet [76] (ProGAN-trained zero-shot, fine-tuned, and joint-training variants)
baselines.fair_comparison: For the continual-learning comparisons, CNNDet (ResNet-50 pretrained on ImageNet and ProGAN) is the backbone for methods other than DyTox. The paper tunes hyperparameters; exemplar-based methods use the same memory budget within each evaluation. Joint training is used as an approximate upper bound.

baselines.name: ConViT [22] (ProGAN-trained zero-shot, fine-tuned, and joint-training variants)
baselines.fair_comparison: The zero-shot and fine-tuning comparisons use the same training strategies as CNNDet. ConViT is ImageNet-pretrained; the paper notes it has about 86M parameters versus about 25M for CNNDet.

baselines.name: NSCIL [75]
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the CNNDet backbone shared with the other non-DyTox methods; hyperparameters were tuned. Memory budgets are shared where a method requires exemplars.

baselines.name: LRCIL [59]
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the CNNDet backbone shared with the other non-DyTox methods; hyperparameters were tuned. Exemplar-based methods use the same memory budget within each evaluation.

baselines.name: iCaRL [60]
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the CNNDet backbone shared with the other non-DyTox methods; hyperparameters were tuned. Exemplar-based methods use the same memory budget within each evaluation.

baselines.name: LUCIR [28]
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the CNNDet backbone shared with the other non-DyTox methods; hyperparameters were tuned. The paper uses LinFC variants in its main comparisons and reports CosFC separately.

baselines.name: DyTox [20]
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses its ImageNet-pretrained ConViT backbone rather than the CNNDet backbone; the paper reports this backbone-size difference. Exemplar-based methods use the same memory budget within each evaluation.

metrics.name: AA (average detection accuracy)
metrics.caveat: Accuracy does not express the precision-recall trade-off; the paper reports mAP alongside it.

metrics.name: AA-M (average deepfake recognition accuracy)
metrics.caveat: Detection accuracy alone does not show how well the model identifies the specific deepfake and real resources; AA-M is reported additionally for that purpose.

controls.name: ProGAN-trained zero-shot reference
controls.detail: CNNDet and ConViT are trained on ProGAN and evaluated directly on the EASY tasks without continual updates.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether continual-learning methods outperform simply applying a detector pretrained on ProGAN to the later tasks.

controls.name: Sequential fine-tuning reference
controls.detail: CNNDet and ConViT are fine-tuned on each new task, without access to old-task data.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether results can be explained by ordinary sequential fine-tuning rather than continual-learning methods that address forgetting.

controls.name: LRCIL without knowledge distillation versus LRCIL-KD
controls.detail: The paper adds a knowledge-distillation term to LRCIL and compares it with the original LRCIL.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the change in performance is associated with adding the distillation mechanism.

controls.name: LUCIR-CosFC versus LUCIR-LinFC
controls.detail: Compares LUCIR with cosine-normalized and regular fully connected layers.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the class-imbalance normalization used by CosFC explains or improves the CDD results; the paper reports that CosFC hurts performance in this setting.

confounds.name: Performance differences may be due to backbone and model size rather than the continual-learning method
confounds.detail: DyTox uses an ImageNet-pretrained ConViT of about 86M parameters, while the other methods use CNNDet with a ResNet-50 of about 25M parameters.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper reports parameter counts and discusses the CNN-versus-ViT comparison, but does not provide a matched-backbone or matched-size comparison.

confounds.name: Class-imbalance effects may explain the results attributed to continual detection behavior
confounds.detail: A method could appear to perform differently because of the class-imbalance correction used in continual multiclass learning, rather than because that correction helps CDD.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare LUCIR-CosFC with LUCIR-LinFC and report AA, AF, and AA-M; the paper finds cosine normalization hurts and explains that predicting a fake as a newer fake class is acceptable for CDD.

evidence_standards.name: Blind human-perception selection for ID-test examples

datasets.name: HySpeFAS
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the challenge train/validation/test split: 3,900 training images (3,380 fake, 520 real), 936 validation images (728 fake, 208 real), and 1,924 test images (test class counts not reported). Evaluates on the challenge test set using ACER, the mean of APCER and BPCER. Images are reconstructed from SSI images with TwIST and have 30 spectral channels; the model concatenates these with RGB images to form 33-channel inputs. Training uses real-sample oversampling and random crop, horizontal flip, cutout, and random-mask augmentation.

datasets.name: CASIA-SURF
datasets.eval_protocol: Within-modal: train and evaluate in the same modality; cross-modal: train on one of RGB, Depth, or IR and evaluate on another. Training uses live faces and Attacks 4–6; validation and testing use live faces and Attacks 1–3. The subject split is 300/100/600 for train/validation/test. Videos are sampled at one frame per 10 frames; preprocessing uses Dlib face detection, PRNet 3D reconstruction/density alignment and masks, followed by resizing cropped face regions to 112×112. Validation is for model and hyperparameter selection; final evaluation is on the test set. Reports ROC/TPR at FPR 10⁻², 10⁻³ and 10⁻⁴ (10⁻⁴ is the main comparison), plus APCER, NPCER and ACER.

datasets.name: Oulu-NPU
datasets.eval_protocol: Pre-train FAS-TD-SF on CASIA-SURF, then fine-tune and evaluate on the four Oulu-NPU protocols: illumination variation (Protocol 1), attack-medium variation (Protocol 2), camera variation (Protocol 3), and all these factors (Protocol 4). Reports APCER, NPCER and ACER.

datasets.name: SiW
datasets.eval_protocol: Pre-train FAS-TD-SF on CASIA-SURF, then fine-tune and evaluate on the three SiW protocols. The paper does not detail the protocol definitions here; it refers readers to the SiW paper. Reports APCER, NPCER and ACER.

datasets.name: CASIA-MFSD
datasets.eval_protocol: Cross-test: train on CASIA-SURF and directly evaluate on CASIA-MFSD, without fine-tuning on CASIA-MFSD. Reports HTER.

datasets.name: AIGCDetectBenchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Setting I: detectors are evaluated on images from 16 generators; all methods except DIRE-D are trained on ProGAN-generated data, while DIRE-D follows its official ADM-trained setup. Report per-generator and mean accuracy; the paper also reports average precision in the Appendix. No evaluation split or item-level preprocessing is specified.

datasets.name: GenImage
datasets.eval_protocol: Detectors are trained on ImageNet real images and fake images generated by SD v1.4, then evaluated on eight generators. Report per-generator and mean accuracy. No evaluation split or item-level preprocessing is specified.

datasets.name: Chameleon
datasets.eval_protocol: Setting II test benchmark: 14,863 real and 11,170 AI-generated images, evaluated with accuracy; the paper also reports fake-image and real-image accuracy separately for detailed analysis, and reports average precision in the Appendix. The test images are curated by discarding images below 448×448, filtering NSFW images with the SD safety checker, removing duplicates by hash, and filtering low image-text similarity with CLIP. AI-generated images are retained as highly realistic only when both of two annotators label them real; real images are likewise retained if they belong to one of the four categories. The paper also evaluates JPEG compression (QF 95, 90, 75, 50) and Gaussian blur (σ 1, 2, 3, 4).

datasets.name: AIGCDetectBenchmark (perturbation evaluation)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate detectors on the benchmark with JPEG compression at QF 95, 90, 75, and 50, and Gaussian blur at σ 1, 2, 3, and 4; report accuracy. Table 6 reports AIDE accuracy averaged over the 16 test sets in B1 for each perturbation.

controls.rules_out: That the full model’s performance is explained without a contribution from its semantic branch.

controls.name: AIDE with combinations of PFE-H, PFE-L, and SFE branches
controls.detail: The ablation table reports configurations using each branch alone and pairs of branches, as well as the full three-branch model, on AIGCDetectBenchmark.

confounds.name: Public benchmark results may reflect easy, non-photorealistic test images rather than robust detection
confounds.detail: The authors note that existing benchmarks commonly use randomly sampled generations without a human-perception Turing Test, so strong results there may not indicate success on deceptively realistic images.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on Chameleon, retaining AI-generated images that both annotators judged to be real, and report detector accuracy there.

confounds.name: Performance declines on Chameleon may be caused by the training setup, such as generator type or image categories, rather than the benchmark’s challenge
confounds.detail: The authors explicitly identify potential biases related to training setups, including generator types and image categories.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate detectors under diverse training conditions, including ProGAN, SD v1.4, and All GenImage training data, and report their Chameleon results.

confounds.name: High average GenImage accuracy may be driven by generators closely related to the training generator
confounds.detail: The authors note that SD v1.5 and Wukong are architecturally similar to SD v1.4, which can allow near-perfect scores and make the average less informative about broader generalization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report results separately across generators, including Midjourney, ADM, and GLIDE, and emphasize performance on these less-similar generators.

evidence_standards.name: Human realism annotation
evidence_standards.detail: The study recruited 20 human workers; each image was assessed independently by two annotators, and an AI-generated image was retained as highly realistic only when both annotators labeled it real.

datasets.name: Deepfake-Eval-2024

For finetuning, use 60% of the data for training and the remaining 40% for evaluation. Commercial models are evaluated on a subset; the top three per modality are then evaluated on the full dataset. datasets.eval_protocol: For adversarial-attack evaluation, use the first 100 Fake and 100 Real videos from the public validation set (30,300 frames total); report video-level success rate only for videos the detector originally predicts correctly. Per-frame attacks are combined into adversarial videos. Detector-specific face tracking, cropping, resizing, and normalization are used. Universal perturbations are trained on 100 DFDC train videos separate from the evaluation videos. The detector AUCs in Table 1 are reported on the DFDC test set.

datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on diffusion-model subsets for DALL·E, Glide variants, ADM, and LDM variants; reports ACC and AP per subset and their mean. Real images are from LAION. datasets.name: GenImage
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on 8 generator subsets (7 diffusion models and BigGAN), each with 6,000–8,000 synthetic images and an equal number of real images from ImageNet; images cover 1,000 classes and vary in size from 128² to 1024². Reports ACC and AP per generator and averages. The paper also uses this set for preprocessing and feature-selection ablations.

datasets.name: DiTFake
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on Flux, PixArt, and SD3 generations, with an equal number of real images from COCO; reports ACC and AP per generator and their mean. The number of images is not specified in the provided text.

datasets.eval_protocol: Deployed on a platform with around 9 million user-generated items per day, detecting human portraits and animals. Reports daily average recall volume at precision levels P95, P98, and P99; compares against the prior online detector at the same precision.

controls.name: Bilinear- and nearest-neighbor resize preprocessing
controls.detail: The preprocessing ablation compares these resize operators with crop-based preprocessing at training and testing on GenImage.
controls.rules_out: Whether the crop-based result is merely an effect of choosing a particular image-preprocessing operator; the comparison tests the paper’s claim that cropping preserves useful artifacts better than resizing.

controls.name: CenterCrop and source-image inference conditions
controls.detail: The GenImage preprocessing ablation compares center cropping and inference without preprocessing (source image) with the main crop-based condition.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported detection result requires a particular inference preprocessing operation; the authors use similar performance across CenterCrop, RandomCrop, and source-image inference to support detection from cropped regions.

controls.name: Augmentation ablations
controls.detail: The paper compares HorizontalFlip and combinations that include or omit ColorJitter, RandomRotation, and RandomMask, reporting average results over 33 test subsets.
controls.rules_out: Whether the improvement requires the proposed augmentations, or whether HorizontalFlip alone or a subset of the proposed augmentations accounts for it.

controls.name: Feature-selection ablation
controls.detail: Compares a source-image Naïve baseline with FFT, DCT, DWT frequency features and Sobel/Laplace edge features; also compares DWT frequency bands.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported performance depends on using DWT high-frequency features rather than source images or another tested low-level feature representation.

confounds.name: The detector may rely on semantic or category cues rather than generalizable low-level artifacts
confounds.detail: A headline gain on test images could reflect semantic differences between training and test samples instead of the claimed artifact-based detection.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors evaluate on GenImage across 1,000 classes and compare against UniFD’s semantic features; they interpret SAFE’s results as robust to semantic variation and emphasize its low-level features.

confounds.name: The apparent generalization may be specific to GANs or to the training generator
confounds.detail: Performance could be high because the detector has learned ProGAN- or GAN-specific cues, without generalizing to other architectures.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Train on ProGAN and evaluate on diffusion-model test sets from Ojha and GenImage, and on the DiTFake test set of Flux, PixArt, and SD3; report results by generator.

confounds.name: The gain may come from feature choice rather than the proposed image transformations
confounds.detail: The headline result could be explained by selecting DWT or another feature representation, rather than by the proposed transformations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper separately ablates preprocessing, augmentations, and feature selection, and tests the transformations as plug-and-play additions to FreqNet and NPR.

datasets.name: All-in-One-DF
datasets.eval_protocol: Randomly split into 60,000 semantically-closest real/fake training pairs and 6,000 evaluation pairs; detectors use a 9:1 training-validation ratio. The attack is evaluated on the 6,000 fake images in the evaluation split. The dataset contains ProGAN, STGAN, and DeepfakeTIMIT fake samples paired with real images; face images are cropped/aligned to 128×128×3. Limited-data experiments train on 1%, 5%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% of the training data; out-of-distribution experiments train on two fake types and evaluate on all three.

controls.rules_out: That low accuracy on attack samples merely reflects poor detection of the original, unattacked fake samples.

confounds.name: Strong-defense results may reflect degraded clean-fake detection after adversarial augmentation with TR-Net samples
confounds.detail: The authors observe that this augmentation substantially compromises detectors' classification of clean fake samples, so low accuracy on TR-Net attack samples could partly reflect a weakened detector rather than attack-specific evasion.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report clean and attacked sample accuracy separately for the strong-defense setting in Table III; the clean-sample results show the degradation rather than concealing it.

evidence_standards.detail: PSNR and SSIM are reported as mean ± standard deviation. The paper specifies no seed/run count, statistical test, or numerical margin for deciding that differences are real.

datasets.name: LSUN Bedroom real-vs-synthetic benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Real images come from LSUN Bedroom; synthetic subsets use ADM, DDPM, iDDPM, PNDM, LDM, Stable Diffusion v1.4, and GLIDE. The paper says each subset contains 42,000 generated images with corresponding real samples and is split into 40,000 training, 1,000 validation, and 10,000 test images; the real test images are consistent across test subsets. Cross-generator evaluations train on one generator and test on others; the degraded-image evaluation trains on LDM and applies low resolution (112 pixels), JPEG compression (quality 65), or Gaussian blur (σ=3) to test images. Reports accuracy and F1-Score.

datasets.name: GAN-generated image evaluation set

Evaluates seven Bi-LORA models trained on diffusion-model subsets on these GAN subsets; no split is specified. Reports accuracy and F1-Score.

Compares models trained on MS COCO vs. SD2 and MS COCO vs. SD2+LaMa; the paper says the evaluation covers two real and 14 fake datasets, including three attacked ones. No per-dataset split or trial count is specified.

metrics.name: Tandem Detection Cost Function (t-DCF)

datasets.name: NTIRE 2026 Challenge test benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Results are reported on the open/public and hidden/private test splits. Each split has 2,500 images; the public split is balanced 1:1 and the private split is approximately 1:1. Half of the real and generated test images are assigned to the robust track. The public test uses 22 transformation types and the private test uses 24. Report clean ROC-AUC on non-distorted images and Robust ROC-AUC on distorted images; final ranking uses average Robust ROC-AUC across the two splits. Submissions were rerun in the official evaluation environment.

confounds.name: Detection could exploit semantic or pairing-related cues rather than forensic artifacts
confounds.detail: Generated images are paired with real counterparts to align semantics, but selecting among similar paired images at evaluation could create an advantage unrelated to detection.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Validation and test use unique images without paired counterparts; the paper says this avoids a potential advantage from selecting between multiple similar images.

confounds.name: Detection could exploit real/fake differences in basic image statistics
confounds.detail: Differences in resolution, aspect ratio, JPEG quality, or similar statistics could act as shortcuts instead of generative artifacts.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The generated-image distributions for resolution, aspect ratio, JPEG compression quality, and other statistics are aligned to those of the real subset.

confounds.name: A detector could identify transformation artifacts correlated with the fake label
confounds.detail: If real and generated images received different degradation pipelines, transformation cues alone could support classification.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The same degradation pipeline is applied to real and generated images in the robust track.

confounds.name: Performance could reflect tuning to known distortion types rather than robustness to other distortions
confounds.detail: A detector might specialize in the distortions it encountered during training or validation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Different distortion sets are used in each dataset split, with progressively more complicated distortions in later challenge stages.

confounds.name: Performance could reflect memorization of training generators rather than generalization to unseen generators
confounds.detail: A detector might recognize artifacts from the training generators without generalizing to newer or unseen models.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Most top-performing open-source models and proprietary generators are reserved for validation and test, with each consecutive split containing a progressively larger share of state-of-the-art models.

confounds.name: Robustness gains could come at the cost of clean-image performance
confounds.detail: A method might improve on distorted images while degrading performance on clean images.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The challenge reports clean ROC-AUC alongside Robust ROC-AUC.

evidence_standards.name: Official ranking by average Robust ROC-AUC
evidence_standards.detail: The final ranking uses average Robust ROC-AUC across the open and hidden test splits, and submissions are rerun in the official evaluation environment. No seed-based uncertainty, confidence intervals, statistical test, or numerical threshold for treating differences as real is specified.

datasets.name: GenImage
datasets.eval_protocol: For cross-generator evaluation, train on the SD v1.4 training subset and evaluate on the evaluating subsets for the other generators; the paper also reports the SD v1.4 subset. For cross-scene evaluation, train on the SD v1.4, ADM, and Midjourney ImageNet-scene subsets and evaluate on the corresponding generators’ evaluating sets in ImageNet and LSUN-Bedroom scenes. Accuracy is reported. Training images are randomly cropped to 224×224 and inference images are center-cropped to 224×224; no other data augmentation is used.

datasets.name: DiffusionForensics (DF)
datasets.eval_protocol: For cross-generator evaluation, train on real images and ADM-generated images, then evaluate on the evaluating sets. The paper specifies 1,000 generated images per generator except Midjourney (100), plus 1,000 real images. For cross-scene evaluation, evaluate the corresponding generators’ DF evaluating sets (LSUN-Bedroom scene) after training on the matching ImageNet-scene GenImage subsets. Accuracy is reported. Training images are randomly cropped to 224×224 and inference images are center-cropped to 224×224; no other data augmentation is used.

controls.name: APN without implicit purification
controls.detail: Remove the mutual-information loss L_mi while leaving the other APN components unchanged.
controls.rules_out: That the full APN result is achieved without a contribution from implicit purification.

controls.name: Direct Swin-Transformer-tiny features with channel-split features
controls.detail: Extract image features directly with Swin-Transformer-tiny, split them into artifact-related and artifact-irrelevant features along the channel dimension, and retain implicit purification.
controls.rules_out: That implicit purification alone, without the proposed explicit purification, accounts for the full result.

controls.name: Frequency-only branch
controls.detail: Remove the spatial branch and its corresponding losses; conduct implicit purification on the remaining frequency branch.
controls.rules_out: That the full result can be attributed to the spatial branch alone.

controls.name: Spatial-only branch
controls.detail: Remove the frequency branch and its corresponding losses; conduct implicit purification on the remaining spatial branch.
controls.rules_out: That the full result can be attributed to the frequency branch alone.

controls.name: Frequency proposal method replaced
controls.detail: Use a ResNet-50 to extract artifact-related features from the input spectra instead of using the proposal method; other unmentioned APN parts remain unchanged.
controls.rules_out: That the frequency-branch result is explained by frequency features alone, without the proposed proposal method.

controls.name: Spatial feature decomposition replaced by channel splitting
controls.detail: Replace the spatial feature decomposition method with splitting along the channel dimension; other unmentioned APN parts remain unchanged.
controls.rules_out: That the spatial-branch result is explained by feature splitting alone, without the proposed decomposition.

confounds.name: The gains come from adding modalities or feature processing, rather than the proposed separation mechanisms
confounds.detail: Cross-domain accuracy could improve simply from using frequency or spatial features, even if the proposed proposal or decomposition mechanisms were not responsible.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare APN against ablations that remove a branch or replace the frequency proposal method or spatial decomposition with simpler feature processing; the paper reports lower average accuracy for these variants.

datasets.name: CASIA-FASD
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated as the CASIA-FASD subset of the expert-annotated X-FAS benchmark, separately from SiW-Mv2. The benchmark subset covers print and replay attacks (24 images, 56 masks). Explanations are compared with annotations using IoU and nIoU; the reported benchmark evaluation thresholds explanations to their top 30% of pixels and averages across masks when an image has multiple masks. Benchmark frames were selected from videos using CLIP features to maximize pairwise dissimilarity among selected frames, with face detection required. FLIP-V was trained on CASIA-FASD; its test-split HTER is reported as 0.11%, but the benchmark evaluation split is not specified. For SPTD concept discovery and importance analysis, two frames per video were randomly selected.

datasets.name: SiW-Mv2
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated as the SiW-Mv2 subset of the expert-annotated X-FAS benchmark, separately from CASIA-FASD. The benchmark subset covers 11 spoof-type categories (753 images, 1,150 masks). Explanations are compared with annotations using IoU and nIoU; the reported benchmark evaluation thresholds explanations to their top 30% of pixels and averages across masks when an image has multiple masks. Benchmark frames were selected from videos using CLIP features to maximize pairwise dissimilarity among selected frames, with face detection required. The FLIP-V model was trained using the SiW-Mv2 intra-protocol; its test-split HTER is reported as 2.49%, but the benchmark evaluation split is not specified. For SPTD concept discovery and importance analysis, two frames per video were randomly selected.

metrics.name: IoU
metrics.caveat: The paper says directly averaging IoU across spoof traces is unfair because the theoretical maximum varies with the ground-truth mask pixel count; it reports nIoU alongside IoU to normalize for this.

metrics.name: Deletion AUC
metrics.direction: Lower is preferred; it measures confidence drop while progressively removing the most important features. Reported alongside insertion AUC.

metrics.name: Insertion AUC
metrics.direction: Higher is preferred; it measures confidence increase while progressively adding the same features back. Reported alongside deletion AUC.

confounds.name: IoU differences may reflect ground-truth mask size rather than explanation quality
confounds.detail: The paper notes that the theoretical maximum IoU varies with the pixel count of the annotated spoof trace, making direct averaging across traces unfair.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report normalized IoU (nIoU), which scales IoU by the ratio of the larger to the smaller of the explanation-mask and annotated-trace pixel percentages, alongside raw IoU.

datasets.name: FaceForensics++ (FF++)
datasets.eval_protocol: Unless otherwise specified, uses the mildly compressed c23 version. For cross-manipulation evaluation, train on three manipulation methods and test on the held-out fourth (DF, FS, F2F, or NT). For cross-dataset evaluation, train on FF++ using all manipulation methods and test on FaceShifter or DeeperForensics. Video-level evaluation uniformly samples non-overlapping clips from each video and averages their predictions. Table 2 uses PGD5 for adversarial training and PGD10 for testing; other evaluations report the specified attacks, including PGD10, RWA, CW2, StatAttack, Universal, and RBB. Training preprocessing includes face detection and alignment, 25-frame clips, random crops resized from 140×140 to 112×112, horizontal flips and grayscale transformation with probability 0.5, and random masking; features are L2-normalized.

controls.name: S1 ablation: deepfake classification loss only
controls.detail: Trains with the deepfake classification loss, omitting both adversarial similarity loss and similarity regularization; evaluated under PGD10 alongside the full method.
controls.rules_out: Comparison with S2 tests whether adding adversarial similarity loss improves robust AUC over classification loss alone.

controls.name: S2 ablation: classification loss plus adversarial similarity loss
controls.detail: Omits similarity regularization while retaining the classification and adversarial similarity losses; evaluated under PGD10 alongside the full method.
controls.rules_out: Comparison with S3 tests whether similarity regularization contributes to robust AUC beyond the other loss components.

confounds.name: Robustness may come at the cost of performance on unperturbed inputs
confounds.detail: The paper notes that adversarial training can reduce performance on normal inputs, so robust scores alone could conceal clean-performance degradation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports no-attack AUC alongside attacked AUC, including on FF++, FaceShifter, and DeeperForensics.

confounds.name: Robustness to common distortions could reflect interactions between training and test distortions
confounds.detail: Training on distortions that overlap with test distortions could explain apparent robustness without generalization to unfamiliar distortions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For the distortion evaluation, limits FF++ training augmentations to horizontal flipping and random cropping for grayscale inputs, then evaluates seven distortion types at five severity levels.
